seite.titel: IYAMBAE Tuner — Spotify in 432 Hz, without converting a file
seite.beschreibung: Menu-bar app for macOS. Retunes your entire system audio in real time — 432 Hz, historical concert pitches or any value you choose, with no change of tempo and no converting. Windows and Linux are built and on their way. We promise you no effect. We give you a slider.
auf.eyebrow: Menu-bar app · macOS · Windows and Linux in the works
auf.titel: Spotify in 432 Hz. Without converting a single file.
auf.vorwort: Netflix, YouTube, your own player just the same. The Tuner sits in the system audio — not in the file.
auf.claim: Nobody knows whether you hear the difference. We don’t either. Least of all us. So: one slider, your ear, a quiet hour.
probe.hilfe: Music on, then drag from 440 to 432.
probe.schirm.aria: Display: shows the beating between the reference tone and the chosen concert pitch as a pulsing waveform.
probe.ohne.1: The test needs JavaScript. But what it is about can also be worked out on paper:
probe.ohne.2: 440 minus 432 is eight hertz. Two tones eight hertz apart cancel each other out eight times a second — that pulsing is what you hear, and it is how people have tuned instruments for centuries: you wait until it stops.
probe.ohne.3: The Tuner does to your whole system audio what the slider here does to two tones.
probe.fuss: Chopin, Nocturne op. 9 no. 2 — public domain. It is retuned here by the same signal core that sits in the Tuner, and at its best setting: the pitch moves, the tempo stays put. That is why it says 100 %, wherever you drag. The display assumes the recording sits at 440 — the Tuner on your own machine does not assume, it measures.

messen.text: Drop a file into the window and find out what concert pitch it really sits on. Free, no account — and the file never leaves your machine, the maths runs in your browser.
bild.alt: The IYAMBAE Tuner’s menu-bar panel on macOS: at the top the switch that turns it on and off, below it the chosen pitch of 432 Hz as the Verdi tuning, then the measured pitch of the music that is playing — 439.7 Hz at 97 per cent confidence — and the correction worked out from it.
bild.hinweis: The Mac version 0.20.1, taken with music playing. The green figure is measured, not assumed: the Tuner hears what the recording actually sits on and works from there to 432 — not from 440, where it only usually sits.
tut.1.text: The sound passes through the Tuner before it reaches your speakers. On macOS and Linux.
tut.2.text: Spotify, YouTube, Netflix, your own player. The Tuner sees the finished sound, not the file.
tut.3.text: Nothing is converted, nothing is stored. The tempo stays as it is.

beweis.1.warum: That is the line between “works with video” and “doesn’t”: the sound stays on the lips. If you would rather have the better sound than the sync, switch to the good engine — 240 ms, useless with picture.
beweis.2.warum: Not claimed, checked: the build script takes the finished library apart and lists every call that leads out of the real-time path. There are none. No memory, no lock — and so nothing that can click in the middle of a track.
beweis.3.warum: Built on macOS 26 with Xcode 26.6. The number stands here because it comes about anew with every build — it is not a badge, it is a measurement taken today.
beweis.4.warum: 440 Hz in, target 432: out come 432.33 Hz with the fast engine and 432.09 Hz with the good one. On macOS, on Linux and on Windows. Spread between them: 0.01 cents.
beweis.5.warum: That is 1077 times real time. The fan does not notice anything is running, and neither does the battery — so there is no reason to switch the Tuner off in between.
beweis.6.warum: This page loads nothing from elsewhere: no font from Google, no analytics, no cookie. The Tuner asks for no account, no email address and sends nothing away. You download a file, and that is that.
beweis.bild.aria: Worked example: a recording sits at 443.1 hertz, the target is 432.0 hertz, that is minus 43.9 cents. The fast engine needs 11 milliseconds for it.
beweis.bild.text: A recording at 443.1 Hz — a value many orchestras play — brought to 432.0. Not a screenshot: calculated, not photographed.

fragen.vorwort: There for whoever asks. Out of the way for whoever wants to download.
frage.hz.1: A concert pitch. It fixes where A4 sits, and everything else follows from it. The standard says 440 Hz; 432 Hz lies eight hertz below that, which is −31.77 cents, or just under a third of a semitone.
frage.hz.2: The Tuner shifts the whole sound by exactly that distance. It does not pick out single notes, and it changes nothing about the music except its pitch.
frage.440.titel: So where does 440 Hz come from?
frage.440.1: From an agreement, not from nature. When Alexander J. Ellis gathered five hundred years of European tuning pitches in 1885, his table ran from 370 to 567 Hz — more than a fifth of spread. The reason was banal: organ pipes were built to the local measure of length, and the “foot” in France was not the “foot” in Saxony. Between the Paris tuning fork of 1822 at 432 Hz and the one of 1855 at 449 Hz lie thirty-three years — and the same city.
frage.440.2: 440 comes from 1834, proposed by Johann Heinrich Scheibler, a silk manufacturer from Krefeld. His reason was as unspectacular as it gets: 440 was the mean around which Viennese pianos drifted between warmth and cold. The conference that turned it into a world standard in 1939 met at BBC headquarters and preferred 440 to 439 because 439 is a prime number and could not be produced from the BBC’s quartz oscillator by chains of dividers.
skala.titel: Concert pitch A4 through the centuries
skala.gross.aria: Scale of tuning pitches from 400 to 480 hertz with four marks: Baroque 415, Scheibler 1834 and London 1939 at 440, Paris tuning fork 1855 at 449, Highland bagpipe 470 to 480.
skala.415: Historically informed performance, one semitone lower
skala.aus.unter: this is where it all happens today
skala.aus.aria: Enlarged detail from 430 to 450 hertz: Milan 1881 at 432, diapason normal Paris 1859 at 435, the standard 440, many orchestras today 443, Berlin Philharmonic under Karajan 445.
skala.liste.415: Historically informed performance — exactly one semitone lower
skala.liste.432: Milan 1881 — Verdi argued for 435 and let 432 stand
brief.zitat: “A piece of childishness that would almost lay itself open to ridicule.”
brief.quelle: Giuseppe Verdi to Arrigo Boito, 8 November 1885. Boito represented Italy at the Vienna pitch conference. Verdi held the 864 vibrations — that is, 432 Hz — to be the more correct ones, but insisting on them would have struck him as ridiculous; the main purpose was one single pitch for everyone. Uniformity mattered more to him than the number. We see it much the same way — and therefore leave the number to you.
frage.forschung.1: A randomised comparison of 432 against 443 Hz — that is, against the tuning today’s orchestras really play at. 43 people, each hearing both. At 432 the pulse fell by three beats a minute, at 443 by one. Pulse wave velocity fell only at 432. The difference between the two tunings held up statistically. The authors themselves write, though, that they cannot say whether this is down to the number 432 or simply to its being lower.
frage.forschung.2: Aravena et al. (2020) compared 432 Hz, 440 Hz and silence before a tooth extraction; 42 people. For anxiety both music groups worked equally well — no difference between 432 and 440. The much-quoted cortisol finding does not survive a check against the full text: the 432 group started out at half the level of the others, and the change was not statistically sound in any of the three groups.
frage.forschung.3: And what speaks against it, so you don’t hear it elsewhere first: these are small studies, no meta-analysis, no independent replication. In the same trial that measured the pulse, the psychological scores did not differ between 432 and 443. And Jebabli et al. (2025) found 440 better for an athletic warm-up.
frage.forschung.4: What follows from that: something has been measured, and it is little. We promise you nothing. Until 01.09.2026 a cortisol figure stood here that we had taken from a study’s abstract. Checking the full text did not bear it out — and then you correct it instead of leaving it standing. The full texts are below under “What others write about it” — read them yourself instead of believing us. And then listen. The only measurement that counts for you, you make with your own ears.
frage.placebo.titel: And what if it is only placebo?
frage.placebo.1: Perhaps it is placebo. That is no objection to listening — it is the reason we put the blind test in front of you instead of telling you what you feel. If it comes out against us, it says so.
frage.placebo.2: And even then: an evening on which you became calmer was a calm evening. Whether the cause lay in the sound or in your having taken an hour for yourself — neither is worth less than the other. We simply do not sell you the one as the other.
frage.digital.1: A widespread picture shows a smooth wave on the left and a staircase on the right. Almost everyone reads it as: digital is jagged. The picture is correct — it just doesn’t show the end.
frage.digital.aria: Three panels: a smooth wave on the left, the same wave as dots with a staircase in the middle, a smooth wave again on the right.
frage.digital.2: The staircase is the intermediate form. On playback a filter sits behind the converter, and it turns the points back into a continuous curve. Below the limit frequency there is exactly one smooth curve through those points.
frage.digital.3: What digital really loses is smaller and duller: a noise floor from the rounding, at 16 bit some 96 decibels below the signal — quieter than the surface noise of any record. Add filter ringing and jitter, audible only in badly built gear.
frage.digital.4: We write this even though it contradicts our own feeling. Anyone who says vinyl sounds different is right — it just isn’t the staircase. It is the cut, the distortion that breathes with the music, and the fact that you can’t play a record in passing.
frage.medizin.1: No. The IYAMBAE Tuner is not a medical device, not a remedy and not a therapeutic instrument. It is a tool that shifts pitch.
frage.medizin.2: It is not intended to detect, treat or alleviate any illness, and we claim that nowhere. If something is wrong with you, see a doctor.
frage.528.titel: What about 528 Hz and the Solfeggio frequencies?
frage.528.1: 528 Hz is not a concert pitch but a single note — roughly a C5. A concert pitch fixes A4, and everything else follows from it. The Tuner shifts the whole sound by an interval; it does not set a single note.
frage.528.2: It can still be worked out: if you want your C5 at 528 Hz, you set A4 to 444.0 Hz — the slider can do that. At A4 = 432 Hz the same C5 sits at about 513.7 Hz.
frage.528.3: About the Solfeggio series itself we say nothing. We know of no source on it that we could pass on here in good conscience, and so we claim neither that it does something nor that it does not.
frage.systeme.1: macOS 14.4 and up — the complete app in the menu bar. Linux with PipeWire 0.3.60 and up — recently with a tray icon as well: pitches under their names, on and off, choice of engine, start at login. Underneath, a LADSPA plugin works in the filter chain. Demonstrated over D-Bus, the click measured: “Verdi tuning” → 432.331 Hz at the output device. Built for Debian 13; for Ubuntu and Zorin it has to be rebuilt.
frage.systeme.2: Under GNOME the tray icon needs the AppIndicator extension once. The package recommends it, and the program says so at startup — instead of staying invisible and leaving the impression that nothing had been installed.
frage.systeme.3: Windows: files yes, system audio not yet. There is its own window, a tray icon and an installer that needs no administrator rights. What it can retune there is files. Not the running system audio — the virtual output device for that is missing.
frage.systeme.4: The reason for this order is technical: Windows lets system audio be listened in on, but not replaced. Anyone who wants to genuinely replace it has to become the output device. On macOS the capture interface does that; on Linux, PipeWire’s filter chain. On Windows it takes a virtual device — a driver of our own is the next step.
frage.telefon.1: Because that is where the sandbox draws its line, not where the effort runs out. On iOS there is no counterpart in any form. On Android you may only capture someone else’s audio if the playing app permits it — and Spotify, Netflix and YouTube do not.
frage.telefon.2: What would be possible is something else: a player of our own that takes the music in hand itself. That is being thought about.
frage.webseite.titel: Why an app and not simply a website?
frage.webseite.1: Because a website has to guess and the app can measure. A page in the browser assumes the recording lies at 440 Hz, calculates the fixed factor 432⁄440 and applies it to everything. With a recording that lies at 443 — a value many orchestras play — you end up at 435 instead of 432.
frage.webseite.2: The Tuner determines the actual tuning of the running sound and works out the distance to the target from that. What lies at 443 is shifted 443 → 432, not 440 → 432. And it reaches the system audio, not just one tab.
frage.webseite.w1.was: That is how far the time-stretch factor is from unity. For an octave it would be 50 %.
frage.webseite.w2.was: The tempo stays. Simply playing back more slowly would turn 120 BPM into 117.8.
frage.webseite.w3.was: of one core with the fast engine — 1077 times real time, measured on Windows.
frage.webseite.w4.was: allocations in the real-time callback. Not claimed: the build script takes the DLL apart and lists every call that leads out. There are none.
frage.latenz.titel: How much latency does it cost?
frage.latenz.1: Shifting pitch without touching tempo costs time — and how much depends on the method. You choose.
frage.latenz.w1.was: Delay line. Fast enough for video and for playing along. The sound stays on the lips.
frage.latenz.w2.was: High Quality (Signalsmith). Sounds better, but is useless with video — a quarter of a second of offset is visible.
frage.latenz.2: The switch crossfades over 25 ms so that the change does not click.
frage.radio.titel: What has this got to do with the radio?
frage.radio.1: If the Tuner is running on the same computer, IYAMBAE Radio can notice it and switch off its own guessing retune. Then the app that measures takes over.
frage.radio.2: You are asked twice in the process: the page asks once, and the Tuner asks you. Without your consent no website learns that you are using it — not even that it is installed. A list of permitted websites in the program code would have been more convenient. It would only have answered the wrong question.
frage.preis.1: This test release costs nothing. It asks for no account, no email address and no payment details — you download a file, and that is that.
frage.preis.2: Nothing has been decided about a price for a later, finished version. If that changes, it will say so here.
frage.daten.1: This page sets no cookies, measures nothing and loads nothing from other people’s servers. The fonts sit on the same server as the page — a link to a font collection in the USA would send your IP address there before you had clicked on anything.
frage.daten.2: The Tuner needs no account and sends nothing away. It processes the sound on the computer itself and records it nowhere. The only interface to the outside is the service for the radio on 127.0.0.1 — it does not leave your computer and answers only if you allow it.
frage.daten.3: The details are in the privacy policy.
wege.vorwort: There are three ways to enjoy 432 Hz. They do not exclude each other — they answer different questions.
wege.1.was: Computers only. Every app, every service, without touching a single file.
wege.1.stand: Where we stand: we are waiting for Apple’s Developer ID. It cannot go into the App Store — it sits too deep in the system for that. Through this site it can.
wege.2.titel: 2 Players that convert as they play
wege.2.was: With any DRM-free source, on the phone too. The catch: you have to own the music and have it stored somewhere.
wege.2.stand: For radio, iyambae.fm covers that need for now. Our own player is planned — but only once we know what we can do differently and better.
wege.3.was: Only with DRM-free material, and honestly only worth it for “lossless”: .flac or .wav.
wege.3.stand: What was once heavily compressed would have to be compressed a second time when converted. With “lossless” the sound is recalculated once — but not compressed a second time. That is the difference.
wege.schluss: For now the focus is on the Tuner and the website. After the test phase we want to offer the software at a fair price. It is time everyone had the freedom to hear music in the tuning they chose themselves. If that isn’t possible in daily life — telephones, doorbells, church bells, sirens, shop music — then at least on your own devices.

spo.seite.titel: Listening to Spotify in 432 Hz — is that possible? Here is how anyway
spo.seite.beschreibung: Spotify has no 432 Hz setting, and there is no sign of one coming. But you do not need it: the sound can be retuned on its way to the speakers — without touching a file and without breaking the terms of use.
spo.eyebrow: The question that has been open for years
spo.kurz: Spotify cannot do it. Your computer can.
spo.lang: A request has been sitting in the Spotify community for years with 188 votes: a setting for tuning. It has never been granted, and nothing suggests that is about to change. But you do not need it. The sound can be retuned on its way between Spotify and your speakers — Spotify notices nothing, because nothing about Spotify is changed.
spo.warum: Why this is not a trick: No more than an equaliser or a volume control changes anything about Spotify, the Tuner does. It sits in the system audio — at the point the sound passes anyway on its way to the speakers. No file is touched, no copy made, nothing circumvented.
spo.wege.titel: What works and what does not
spo.w1.name: Retune the system audio — Mac
spo.w1.text: Spotify plays as usual. The sound goes through the IYAMBAE Tuner, and 432 comes out of the speakers. It applies to everything at once — Spotify, YouTube, Netflix, your own player. One switch, not a thousand conversions.
spo.w2.name: Converting Spotify’s offline files
spo.w2.text: What Spotify stores offline is encrypted. It is not a music file that happens to sit elsewhere — it cannot be read outside the app at all. No converter in the world gets at it, ours included. That is not a weakness of some software, that is the deal: you rent, you do not buy.
spo.w3.name: Recording it and retuning that
spo.w3.text: Technically conceivable, legally not: circumventing copy protection is separately regulated, and we do not help with it. It would also be the worse way — a great deal of work for a result that starts over with every new track.
spo.w4.name: On the phone
spo.w4.text: Android and iPhone let no app at another app’s sound. That is not a question of effort, that is a wall in the operating system — and it holds for every provider, not just for us. On the phone you still have the radio in your browser, where the retuning happens in the page itself.
spo.f1.text: No. There are two ways to make something sound lower: play it slower — then pitch and tempo move — or shift only the pitch. The Tuner does the second. The tempo stays at 100 per cent, wherever you drag the slider.
spo.f2.titel: Am I breaking the terms of use?
spo.f2.text: As we understand it, no: nothing is copied, nothing decrypted, nothing passed on. What is changed is the sound already coming out of your speakers — just as any equaliser does. We are not legal advisers, though, and terms can change.
spo.f3.text: Nothing is re-compressed. The sound is computed once, on its way to the speaker — no file comes into being that would be made lossy a second time. How exactly that works is under sample rate and pitch.
spo.f4.titel: How do I know it works?
spo.f4.text: Listen for yourself, blind: in the listening test you get the same passage twice, tuned differently, and you guess. Five trials, honest scoring — even when the result goes against us.
spo.danach.text: The Tuner is a test release for macOS — free, no account. Install it, switch it on, start Spotify. And if you want to know first what your music sits on: measure it.
sam.seite.titel: 44.1 kHz is not a pitch — sample rate and 432 Hz are two different things
sam.seite.beschreibung: “How do I set my sound card to 432 Hz?” — you don’t. Sample rate and concert pitch are two different things, and the mix-up explains dozens of forum questions. Here is what each number means.
sam.eyebrow: The most common mistake in the field
sam.vorwort: “How do I set my sound card to 432 Hz?” — you don’t. The number on your sound card and the concert pitch of your music are two different things that happen to share a unit. That explains more forum questions than anything else in this subject.
sam.karte.a.text: How often the sound was measured — 44,100 snapshots per second. A property of the recording, not of the music. It says nothing about how high or low anything sounds.
sam.karte.b.text: How fast the air vibrates — at one particular note, the A above middle C. A property of the music. It says nothing about how finely anything was recorded.
sam.merksatz: A film has 24 frames per second. How fast the actor walks is another matter entirely.
sam.fragen.titel: The questions that follow from this
sam.f1.titel: Can I set my sound card to 432 Hz?
sam.f1.text: No — the setting you find there is something else. Sound cards know 44.1 kHz, 48 kHz, 96 kHz and similar values. Those are sample rates. 432 would not be a valid entry there, and even if you could type it in, no 432 Hz concert pitch would come of it — only an unusable recording.
sam.f1.was: What you are actually after is done by a program that sits between the music and the speaker and shifts the pitch. That is exactly what the IYAMBAE Tuner is.
sam.f2.titel: How do I convert a song from 44,100 kHz to 432 Hz?
sam.f2.text: The question stands in that form in dozens of forums, and it cannot be answered, because it puts together two quantities that have nothing to do with each other. The sample rate stays where it is. What changes is the pitch of the content — from 440 (or wherever the recording really sits) to 432. That is 1.8 per cent lower, or 31.8 cents.
sam.f3.titel: But if I change the sample rate, it does sound lower?
sam.f3.text: Yes — and that is exactly the confusion that keeps the error alive. If you play a file recorded at 44,100 back at 43,309, it sounds lower. But it also runs slower: a four-minute piece suddenly takes four minutes and four seconds.
sam.f3.wann: It is still a clean route, if that is what you want: not a single number is recalculated, only a different rate is written into the file header. Bit-exact, without any loss — paid for with the tempo. Anyone who wants to keep the tempo cannot avoid the fact that something has to be computed.
sam.f4.titel: Does the music lose quality when it is retuned?
sam.f4.text: With lossless material — FLAC, WAV, AIFF, ALAC — the sound is recalculated once and then stored losslessly again. No second compression step, no stacking of artefacts.
sam.f4.lossy: With MP3 or AAC it is different: what has already been heavily compressed would have to be compressed a second time when written back. That is why lossless source material is not a nicety here, it is the difference.
sam.f5.titel: And what about “my track is in 432 Hz”?
sam.f5.text: Strictly speaking that is off as well, but it is a useful shorthand. A piece of music does not have one frequency — it has many, at once, constantly changing. What is meant is always the reference note: if the A above middle C sits at 432 Hz, every other note sits accordingly. A tuning is a grid, not a single note.
sam.tab.d2: amount of data per second after compression
sam.tab.e2: vibration of the reference note A
sam.tab.fuss: The first four rows describe the file. The last two describe the music. That both are measured in hertz is the whole reason for the confusion.

sam.danach.text: Drag a file into the window — the measuring tool tells you the concert pitch in a few seconds. Free, in the browser, nothing is uploaded.
ber.seite.titel: Corrections — what was wrong on this site
ber.seite.beschreibung: Every statement on these pages that turned out to be wrong — with the date, the old wording, and what stands there now. We correct in public instead of changing things quietly.
ber.vorwort: Every statement on these pages that turned out to be wrong — with the date, the old wording, and what stands there now. We do not change things quietly.
ber.warum: In a field where almost everyone overstates, the only currency that counts is checkability. A site that was always right has either never claimed anything concrete or tidied its mistakes away. We would rather put ours on display. If you find a correction here that we have missed, send it to us — it will end up on this page.
ber.1.wo: Home page · FAQ “What has been measured so far?”
ber.1.titel: A cortisol figure the data do not support
ber.1.alt: For salivary cortisol the 432 group came out markedly lower than both others: 0.49 against 1.35 and 1.59 µg/dL.
ber.1.neu: On anxiety both music groups worked equally well — no difference between 432 and 440. The much-quoted cortisol finding does not survive a check against the full text.
ber.1.warum: We had taken the numbers from the abstract of the study, not from the data. Reading the full text showed: the 1.35 is the starting value of the 440 group, not its final one — we had mixed up beginning and end. And the changes within the groups were none of them statistically sound; the 432 group started out at half the value already. With fifteen people per group, the difference in final values is in all likelihood an accident of how the groups were drawn.
ber.1.quelle: Aravena et al., J Appl Oral Sci 28 (2020), e20190601 · independent review, University of Padua, 2023
ber.2.wo: Home page · sound sample and scale
ber.2.titel: Milan was 1881, and 432 was not Verdi’s number
ber.2.alt: Milan 1880, Verdi’s number · Milan 1880, the number Verdi stood for
ber.2.neu: Milan 1881 — Verdi stood for 435 and let 432 pass
ber.2.warum: Two errors in one line. The Congresso dei Musicisti Italiani met in June 1881, not 1880. And Verdi was indeed the most prominent advocate of a lower pitch — but his favourite was the French 435; he accepted 432 only, on the grounds that the difference was “so small, almost imperceptible to the ear”. The battle cry “Verdi tuning” for 432 was not coined until 1988, a good eighty years after his death.
ber.2.quelle: Gazzetta musicale di Milano, 13 Nov 1881 · Carteggio Verdi–Ricordi 1882–1885 · Rosenberg, J Popular Music Studies 33 (2021)
ber.3.wo: Home page · FAQ, the same answer
ber.3.titel: A caveat missing that the authors state themselves
ber.3.warum: On the study that found a lower pulse at 432 Hz, one sentence was missing: the authors write themselves that they cannot say whether this is down to the number 432 or simply to its being lower. The finding stands — the qualification belongs with it, and it was not there.
ber.3.quelle: Hohneck et al., BMC Complement Med Ther (2025), PMID 39844155
ber.4.titel: A version number twenty releases old
ber.4.neu: softwareVersion: the number from the download link, automatically
ber.4.warum: It was never visible: the entry sits in the structured data and is read only by machines. That is precisely why it went stale unnoticed — for search engines the Tuner was a 0.1.0 for months while the page offered a 0.21.1. A number nobody sees is a number nobody checks. It now comes from the same line as the button; if the link is missing, the build stops.
ber.5.wo: iyambae.fm · status line of the player
ber.5.warum: The radio assumes for every station that it sits at 440 and takes off a flat 1.8 per cent. Nothing is measured there — and three other places on the same page say so explicitly. A word in the status line that contradicts that costs more than truth; it devalues the very argument by which we set the Tuner apart from everything else.
ber.regel.1.text: Every factual statement that was wrong — figures, years, attributions, technical details. Not typos, rewordings, or changes of mind about design.
ber.regel.2.text: A correction that does not show the error is not one. So both stand here side by side — and the old sentence is not prettied up.
ber.regel.3.text: Write to us. We check it against the primary source, not against an abstract — that was exactly the error in the first entry above. If it holds, it comes here, with a date.
elt.seite.titel: 432 Hz and 528 Hz — what parents of music students should know
elt.seite.beschreibung: Your child is learning an instrument, and somewhere you came across the number 432. What is musically true about it, what isn’t, and what it means for lessons — with figures, sources and no promises.
elt.eyebrow: For parents, teachers and anyone who gets asked
elt.titel: What 432 Hz and 528 Hz are really about
elt.vorwort: Your child is learning an instrument, and somewhere you came across the number 432 — in a video, in an app, in a conversation after the lesson. Here is what is musically true about it, what isn’t, and what it means for lessons.
elt.kurz.1: Concert pitch is an agreement, not a constant of nature. That it can be something other than 440 Hz is historically correct.
elt.kurz.2: There is a real, small history behind 432 Hz — and a great many claims that do not hold up.
elt.kurz.3: For lessons the question is practical, not philosophical. Listening: harmless. Retuning: a decision with consequences.
elt.strahl.1: When an orchestra tunes, it agrees on a single note: the a′, the reference pitch. Everything else follows from it. Since 1955 that has been standardised at 440 Hz.
elt.wien.strahl2: Diese Norm ist jünger und lockerer, als die meisten glauben. Vor 1859 gab es gar keine — erhaltene Orgeln und Stimmgabeln zeigen ein a′ zwischen etwa 390 und 505 Hz. Und auch heute halten sich viele Orchester nicht daran: Deutschland und Österreich liegen üblicherweise bei 442 bis 443 Hz, die Wiener Philharmoniker seit den 1980er Jahren bei etwa 444.
elt.strahl.aria: Number line of reference pitches from 432 to 444 hertz
elt.wien.bu: Ein Halbton sind 100 Cent. Zwischen 432 und dem Wiener 444 liegt also fast ein halber Halbton — deutlich mehr als der Abstand, um den es in der Diskussion meist geht (432 gegen 440: 31,8 Cent). Ein Kind in Wien wächst ohnehin nicht mit exakt 440 auf.
elt.hist.1: The historical core is genuine, but small. A congress of Italian musicians in Milan recommended 432 in 1881, and an Italian military decree of 1884 prescribed it for military bands. As early as 1885 an international conference — in Vienna, of all places — settled on 435, and with that the episode was effectively over.
elt.hist.2: Verdi is often called as the star witness. He did argue for a lower pitch, but his preference was the French 435; he accepted 432 with the remark that the difference was “so small, almost imperceptible to the ear”. The term “Verdi tuning” for 432 was only coined in 1988, a good eighty years after his death, as part of a political campaign.
elt.hoert.1: The difference between 432 and 440 is 31.8 cents, just under a third of a semitone. In direct comparison — the same piece, once each way — that is clearly audible; the discrimination threshold lies at a few cents.
elt.hoert.2: Without a comparison practically nobody can identify it. Absolute pitch is rare, and even those who have it hear a pitch, not a number. Music tuned lower can subjectively feel warmer or calmer — because it is lower, not because 432 is a special number. At 431 or 433 the impression would be the same.
elt.solf.1: These numbers often come up in the same breath as 432, although they have an entirely different origin — and do not even fit together with 432.
elt.solf.2: The list of six “Solfeggio frequencies” (396, 417, 528, 639, 741, 852) first appears in a book from 1999. Its author states that he received them in a vision, derived from the verse numbers of the Book of Numbers. With the medieval solfeggio of Guido of Arezzo they share nothing but the syllable names.
elt.solf.3: And arithmetically: 528 Hz is the c″ — but only if the a′ sits at around 444 Hz. At a reference pitch of 432 the c″ lies at 513.7 Hz. So anyone listening “in 432 Hz” is precisely not listening to 528. The two numbers rule each other out.
elt.pruef.titel: What is often claimed — and what can be checked
elt.pruef.a.was: People used to tune lower than today
elt.pruef.a.wie: But not uniformly, and not at 432. The documented values scatter between roughly 390 and 505 Hz, depending on place, century and instrument.
elt.pruef.b.was: Mozart, Hendrix or Bob Marley played in 432
elt.pruef.b.wie: Mozart’s circle sits at around 421 Hz. Hendrix tuned a whole semitone lower — 100 cents, not 32; that is a transposition, not a question of reference pitch. Marley’s instruments were built fixed to 440.
elt.pruef.c.wie: The Schumann resonance lies at about 7.83 Hz and fluctuates. Raised by octaves it gives roughly 501 Hz, not 432.
elt.pruef.d.was: 440 Hz was imposed for political motives
elt.pruef.d.wie: 440 Hz was already recommended in Stuttgart in 1834, long before the conference of 1939 — which was organised by the British, with French participation.
elt.pruef.e.was: 528 Hz acts on cells or on DNA
elt.pruef.e.wie: This claim comes from the same book of 1999. There is no published experimental basis for it; the frequently cited chain of evidence dissolves on inspection.
elt.forsch.1: It is well established that music as such reduces tension — before medical procedures, for instance. There are systematic reviews for that with several thousand participants.
elt.forsch.2: That does not hold for a specific advantage of 432 over 440. On that there are only small pilot studies with eight to fifty-four participants, mostly from a single research group, without independent replication. The largest study so far (2026, 162 participants) even found a rather unfavourable picture for 432. There is no meta-analysis.
elt.forsch.3: That is not a statement against 432 Hz — it is the observation that the evidence for the big promises is missing. As a musical option, the lower tuning remains valid, interesting and entirely harmless.
elt.forsch.knopf: What we have corrected here ourselves
elt.unt.vor: This is where the question becomes concrete — and where a conversation with the teacher pays off, because the answer depends on the instrument.
elt.unt.a.was: Listening to music at home in 432 Hz: entirely harmless. It is the same music, a little lower.
elt.unt.b.was: Can be tuned to any reference pitch. But someone who practises alone at 432 and then sits at 443 in the ensemble trains their ear on a reference that does not apply when playing together.
elt.unt.c.was: Are built around one reference pitch and adjustable only within narrow limits. Switching to 432 is not a matter of taste here; it comes at the cost of intonation.
elt.unt.d.was: The reference pitch is not a setting but a job for the piano tuner — and going back and forth frequently is neither sensible nor cheap.
elt.unt.e.was: The practical heart of it: recitals, exams, orchestra and accompaniment all run on the customary pitch. A child working towards that needs a reliable reference there.
elt.unt.fazit: As a listening experience there is nothing against 432 Hz. As a practice tuning for a child who plays with others, practical considerations speak against it.
elt.probe.1: The most honest way is your own comparison, and a blind one — that is, without knowing which version is playing. This is exactly the point at which many claims grow quieter.
elt.probe.2: The listening test runs in the browser, without signing up and without installing anything. It claims nothing and reports honestly — including when you hear no difference.
elt.probe.radio: And for anyone who wants to experience the difference not in a test setup but in music they actually like: IYAMBAE FM is an ad-free internet radio that retunes any of its stations to 432 Hz on request.
elt.quell.1: Historical pitches: Alexander J. Ellis, “On the History of Musical Pitch” (1880); Bruce Haynes, A History of Performing Pitch (2002, around 1,400 instruments measured). Milan 1881 and Verdi’s position: Gazzetta musicale di Milano, 13 Nov 1881, and the Verdi–Ricordi correspondence. Viennese pitch: Clemens Hellsberg, “Gedanken zum Stimmton” (2016). Solfeggio frequencies: L. G. Horowitz and J. S. Puleo, Healing Codes for the Biological Apocalypse (1999). Research: Cochrane reviews on music and anxiety (2013/2021) and the individual studies on 432 and 528 Hz up to 2026.
elt.quell.2: All frequency and cent figures have been recalculated. This page deliberately makes no claims about health effects — the basis for such claims is missing.
elt.strahl.2: This standard is younger and looser than most people think. Before 1859 there was none at all — surviving organs and tuning forks show an a′ between roughly 390 and 505 Hz. And even today many orchestras do not keep to it: the New York Philharmonic tunes to 442 Hz, Berlin and Vienna sit higher still. Playing at exactly 440 is more the exception.
elt.strahl.bu: A semitone is 100 cents. Between 432 and 440 lie 31.8 of them — between 432 and the 444 Vienna uses, almost half a semitone. Whichever orchestra your child ends up playing with, it is unlikely to be exactly 440.
gtr.seite.titel: Tuning a guitar to 432 Hz — and why a half step is something else
gtr.seite.beschreibung: Tuning down a half step is not 432 Hz. One is 100 cents, the other 31.8 — a good three times as much. Here are the string frequencies, the difference to E♭, and what the Hendrix argument is worth.
gtr.eyebrow: The mix-up that sits on every fretboard
gtr.vorwort: In the forums both sentences stand side by side as if they meant the same thing: “tune down a half step” and “tune to 432”. They do not mean the same thing. A good two thirds of a semitone lie between them — more than enough to pull any ensemble apart.
gtr.karte.a.text: Roughly an eighth of a semitone. You hear it in a direct comparison, but no fingering shifts and no string goes slack.
gtr.karte.b.text: A whole semitone. E becomes E♭, and every chord name becomes another one. The strings get noticeably softer.
gtr.merk: Both sound lower. One is a good three times as low as the other.
gtr.tab.fuss: The middle column is the first one times 432 divided by 440 — the same factor everywhere, 0.9818. The right-hand one is the first times the twelfth root of a semitone. Two different calculations, two different results, and that is why the two columns do not match.
gtr.wie.1: Look for the reference pitch in your tuner. Almost every clip-on has it, usually labelled Calibration, A4 or Pitch. It comes set to 440.
gtr.wie.2: Set it to 432. Usually with the same button you otherwise use to switch modes, held down. Eight steps down.
gtr.wie.3: Now tune as usual. E, A, D, G, B, E — the device does the arithmetic for you. You only need the numbers above if your tuner has no reference pitch; then you type them into a tuning app.
gtr.wie.4: You do not have to worry about the neck. 1.8 per cent less tension is a fraction of what one gauge lighter would do. With E♭ or lower it looks different.
gtr.hendrix.1: The argument turns up in every other thread: Hendrix played at 432, that is why it sounds like that. The recordings really do sit lower than concert pitch — but by roughly a half step, which is about 100 cents. That is the left-hand column above, not the middle one.
gtr.hendrix.2: Why he did it is no mystery: a half step less tension makes bending easier, and it suits the voice. It was common among guitarists of those years and has stayed common.
gtr.hendrix.3: That he had 432 in mind while doing so — for that we know of no source, and the numbers argue against it. Between 432 and a half step down lie 68 cents. That is more than two thirds of a semitone; hear them side by side and you will not confuse them.
gtr.mit.1: Your guitar now sits at 432. The recording you want to play along with sits at 440 — and so things sound together that do not belong together. Either you tune back, or the recording comes to you.
gtr.mit.2: That is exactly what the IYAMBAE Tuner is for: it shifts the sound on its way to the speaker without touching the tempo. What comes out of the computer then sits where your instrument sits.
gtr.mit.3: One question remains worth asking: does the recording sit at 440 at all? Many do not — tape machines ran imprecisely, and whoever found a piano in the studio took its tuning. Drag the file into the measuring tool and you will know instead of assuming.
sol.seite.titel: The Solfeggio frequencies — where the numbers come from
sol.seite.beschreibung: 528, 396, 639 — the nine Solfeggio numbers come from a book published in 1999 and from a numerological reading, not from the Middle Ages. Here is their origin, the arithmetic behind them, and why 528 and 432 do not fit together.
sol.kurz: The nine numbers come from a book published in 1999.
sol.kurz2: Not from the Middle Ages, not from a measurement, not from a lost manuscript. They were published in Healing Codes for the Biological Apocalypse by Joseph Puleo and Leonard Horowitz — derived from a numerological reading of a chapter in the Book of Numbers.
sol.vorwort: This page does not tell you what to listen to. Where a number comes from does not decide what it does to you — you decide that, and nobody has any business telling you otherwise. It only tells you where the number comes from, because that is stated wrongly in a great many places and because it can be checked.
sol.zeit.1: Guido of Arezzo takes the opening syllables of the hymn Ut queant laxis as names for scale degrees: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. That is where the word Solfeggio comes from. No frequencies appear in it — the concept does not exist yet.
sol.zeit.2: Marin Mersenne measures for the first time how often a string vibrates per second. Only from here on can a note be written as a number at all — six hundred years after Guido.
sol.zeit.3: Stuttgart settles on 440, Paris fixes 435 by decree. The pitch is argued over because it differed everywhere.
sol.zeit.4: The unit gets its name: hertz, after Heinrich Hertz. So every number with “Hz” after it is younger than that.
sol.zeit.5: Puleo and Horowitz publish six numbers — 396, 417, 528, 639, 741, 852 — and assign them to Guido’s six syllables.
sol.zeit.6: Three more are added: 174, 285, 963. They are not in the original book and come from others.
sol.zeit.fuss: Nearly a thousand years lie between Guido and the numbers. That is not a detail at the margin — it is the heart of the matter. A medieval syllable cannot carry a frequency when in its own time there was neither frequency measurement nor a unit for it.
sol.bau.1: Puleo describes obtaining them through a digit-sum calculation from figures in Numbers 7. You do not have to believe that in order to check it — the numbers carry the arithmetic themselves.
sol.bau.2: Three, six, nine — over and over, without a single exception. No measured value in the world comes out like that. This is not an accusation; it is an observation about the kind of number: they are constructed, not found. Anyone who wants to continue the series needs no laboratory for it, only the rule.
sol.konflikt.1: This is where it becomes practical — and the reason this page sits on a 432 site. The two most popular numbers contradict each other. You cannot have both at once.
sol.rechnung.1: If the A sits at 432 Hz, the C above it sits at 513.74 Hz.
sol.rechnung.2: If the A sits at 440 Hz, the C above it sits at 523.25 Hz.
sol.rechnung.3: For the C to sit at 528 Hz, the A has to sit at 444 Hz.
sol.konflikt.2: So 528 is the C of a tuning with A = 444 — a tuning that sits higher than the usual 440, not lower. It is the opposite of what 432 stands for.
sol.konflikt.3: The gap is no hair’s breadth: between 528 and the C of a 432 tuning lie 47 cents, almost a quarter tone. Anyone who plays both one after the other hears it.
sol.merk: Set your track to 432 and you do not have 528 in it. You have 513.74.
sol.dna.1: It stands on thousands of pages, usually without a source. It traces back to the same book of 1999, which in turn relies on work that never appeared in a peer-reviewed journal and that nobody has repeated.
sol.dna.2: We do not make that claim — because it is not evidenced, not because we take it for a quiet secret. What you experience yourself while listening is another matter: that belongs to you and needs no evidence.
sol.dna.3: What we do not do: promise you an effect. The Tuner is not a remedy and does not want to be one. It shifts pitch, and what comes of that is yours to decide.
sol.pruef.1: Does your 528 file even sit at 528? Many recordings sold that way are ordinary material at 440. Drag a file into the measuring tool — it tells you in a few seconds where it really sits, and nothing is uploaded.
sol.pruef.2: Can you hear the difference? In the listening test you get the same passage twice, tuned differently, and you guess. Five rounds, honest arithmetic — even when the result goes against us.
hoer.seite.titel: Can you hear the difference between 432 and 440 Hz? — blind test
hoer.seite.beschreibung: A blind test in two rounds: first 432 against 440 Hz, then 432 against 433. The same excerpt, random order, five trials. You find out what you really hear — and what the number has to do with it. Free, no account.
hoer.vorwort: The same excerpt twice, tuned differently, the order shuffled. You say which one sounds lower. Five trials per round — and at the end it says what the result is worth.
hoer.hinweis.start: Listen to both — as often as you like. Headphones help; laptop speakers barely reproduce low notes.
hoer.placebo: Perhaps it is placebo. That is no objection to listening — it is the reason there is a blind test here and not a claim.
hoer.wie.titel: What is measured here — and what is not
hoer.wie.r1.text: 31.8 cents apart — just under a third of a semitone. The threshold at which people tell two pitches apart in direct comparison is around 3 to 12 cents. Almost everyone passes this round, and that is not imagination but physics.
hoer.wie.r2.text: 4.0 cents — at the threshold. This round answers the real question: does the number 432 have a sound of its own, or do you only hear that something is lower? Anyone who experiences 432 as special ought to be able to tell it from 433.
hoer.wie.sauber.text: Both excerpts run through the same signal core — the 440 one too, at factor 1.0. Otherwise you would hear the processing instead of the pitch, and that would be the real giveaway.
hoer.wie.sauber.pegel: The loudness difference is measured and comes to 0.03 dB between 432 and 440, and 0.01 dB between 432 and 433. That is far below anything a person hears — so there is nothing to give it away but the pitch itself. Loudness is the commonest quiet cheat in listening tests: people take the louder one for the better one.
hoer.wie.sauber.zufall: The order is shuffled anew for every trial, and the scoring says what small numbers are worth: five out of five by pure guessing happens 3.1 % of the time, four out of five or better 18.8 %.
hoer.wie.ehrlich.titel: What a result does not prove
hoer.wie.ehrlich.text: Five trials are five trials. Anyone who gets them all in round 2 may have a very fine ear — or may have been lucky. And anyone who misses does not therefore hear badly: 4 cents is too little for almost everyone. The test says something about this afternoon, not about you.
hoer.wie.ehrlich.geschmack: And it says nothing about which one you prefer. That is a different question, it is a matter of taste, and only you can answer it.
hoer.danach.text: If you want to know what your own music sits on, measure it — free, in your browser, nothing is uploaded. And if you want to hear it differently for good, that is what the IYAMBAE Tuner does: for everything coming out of your speakers, without touching a file.
hoer.wort.start: Listen to both — as often as you like.
hoer.wort.fehler: The sound cannot be prepared in this browser. Try a different one.
hoer.wort.zufallSatz: That well or better comes up by blind guessing {p} % of the time.
hoer.wort.r1gut: You hear 31.8 cents — just under a third of a semitone. You are not imagining it. Almost everyone passes this round.
hoer.wort.r1mau: Almost everyone passes this round. If it goes wrong here it is usually the speakers — try headphones.
hoer.wort.r2gut: Four cents. That is remarkable — and rare. Over five trials it may also have been luck; the number below says how often.
hoer.wort.r2mau: The difference is audible. The exact number is not. Four cents lie below the threshold for almost everyone — and that is the honest finding: you hear that something is lower. That it is exactly 432.0 is heard by nobody.
mess.seite.titel: What pitch is my music tuned to? — measure it free
mess.seite.beschreibung: Drop a music file into the window and find out what concert pitch it really sits on — 432, 440, 443 Hz or somewhere between. The maths runs in your browser: your file never leaves your machine. Free, no account, no uploading.
mess.titel: What concert pitch is your music on?
mess.vorwort: Drag a file here. In a few seconds you will know what the recording is really tuned to — and how far that is from 432 Hz.
mess.zone.klein: MP3, M4A, WAV, FLAC, OGG — whatever your browser can play
mess.bruecke.text: This page tells you what your music sits on. The IYAMBAE Tuner changes it — for everything coming out of your speakers: Spotify, YouTube, your own player, without touching a single file. And it measures the same way, instead of assuming 440.
mess.hoertest: And if you want to know what your ears can do: in the blind test you hear the same passage twice, tuned differently, and guess — five trials, with honest scoring.
mess.frage.hochladen.text: No. The maths runs in your browser, on your device. The file is not transmitted, not buffered and not stored. You can disconnect from the network once this page has loaded — the measuring keeps working.
mess.frage.kammerton.text: Concert pitch is the reference tone a piece is tuned to — given as the frequency of the A above middle C. 440 Hz is the usual value today, set in 1955 by the standard ISO 16. Anyone listening at 432 Hz has their material tuned about 1.8 per cent lower: 31.8 cents, just under a third of a semitone.
mess.frage.abweichung.titel: Why isn’t my music on 440 Hz?
mess.frage.abweichung.text: Because almost no recording sits exactly there. Orchestras today often tune to 442 or 443 Hz, historical performance practice to 415, older tapes have changed speed over decades, and digitising either corrects for it or does not. The 440 are a standard, not a law of nature.
mess.frage.genau.text: On pure tones from 432 to 445 Hz the error stays below 0.2 cents, on real music below 1 cent — checked against recordings we detuned on purpose, so the truth was known. A cent is one hundredth of a semitone; people tell apart five to ten at best.
mess.frage.genau.wie: The maths works on the peaks in the frequency spectrum: every tone is asked how far it sits from the nearest equal-tempered step, and all of them together give a circular mean — circular, because +49 and −51 cents are the same tuning. It is the same method the IYAMBAE Tuner uses to estimate the source pitch.
mess.frage.grenze.titel: What can this measurement not do?
mess.frage.grenze.text: It only identifies the tuning to within a semitone. Baroque pitch 415.3 Hz sits exactly one semitone below 440 — to the maths both look the same, and it reports 440. That is not a weakness of the method but lies in the matter itself: a semitone lower is the same tuning, just a different key. Anyone measuring historical recordings has to keep that in mind.
mess.frage.grenze.mehr: And it needs tones. With pure percussion, speech or noise the readings cancel each other out — then the page reports a low confidence instead of an invented number.
mess.frage.sicherheit.titel: What does the confidence percentage mean?
mess.frage.sicherheit.text: It says how much the samples from the piece agree. We measure at up to 24 places spread across the whole piece and compare them. From 35 per cent the estimate counts as sound — with clean musical material it is usually above 90. If it falls below, the page says so explicitly.
mess.frage.formate.text: Anything your browser can play: MP3, M4A/AAC, WAV, FLAC, OGG, Opus. The soundtrack of a video too, if you drop the video file in. Very long files take a moment — the measuring is still spread across the whole piece, not just the beginning.
mess.wort.fehlerLesen: Your browser cannot read this file. Try MP3, M4A, WAV or FLAC.
mess.wort.zuKurz: The recording is too short to measure.
mess.wort.keinKlang: There is no tone here that would have a tuning.
mess.wort.satzUnsicher: No tuning is discernible here — the readings contradict each other.
mess.wort.satzFern: The nearest is {kammerton} Hz ({name}), but {cent} cents off.
mess.wort.warnUnsicher: The confidence is below 35 per cent. With percussion, speech or a very dense arrangement this number does not hold — try another recording.
rueck.frage.test: Add this result to our statistics, anonymously?
rueck.dazu.test: What is sent: the round and the number of hits. Nothing about you, no identifier, no cookie. A result at guessing level counts too — that one especially.
